\chapter{The Market}
\label{ch:te-the-market}
\hlchaptermodality{72}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can buy something in a Telugu shop, ask the price, and thank the seller.}

Complete TE-C72-bargain and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[aṅgaḍi]{\te{అంగడి} (aṅgaḍi) — a shop}

\label{lesson:TE-C72-shop}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{alluḍu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{అంగడి}}
\textbf{\te{అంగడి}} (\emph{aṅgaḍi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a shop\textquotedblright{}.

\te{అంగడి} is a shop — one counter, one family behind it, and everything a \te{గ్రామం} needs on the shelves.

It is inherited, and it is the older and homelier of the two words available. City Telugu will as often reach for a borrowed word for a store, but the \te{అంగడి} is the one at the end of the \te{బాట}.

You are known in an \te{అంగడి}. Nobody there opens with a price; they open by asking whether your household is well.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One. The place the rest of this chapter happens in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aṅgaḍi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{aṅgaḍi}, then \emph{grāmaṁ}, and say which one sits inside the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{అంగడి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a shop\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ḍabbu]{\te{డబ్బు} (ḍabbu) — money}

\label{lesson:TE-C72-money}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{aṅgaḍi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{డబ్బు}}
\textbf{\te{డబ్బు}} (\emph{ḍabbu}) — \textquotedblleft{}money\textquotedblright{}.

\te{డబ్బు} is money. You have said it once already without being told what it was: \te{డబ్బు} \te{లేదు}, there is no money, turned up early as an example of how \te{లేదు} denies that a thing exists. Here is the word itself.

It is a borrowing, from the name of a small copper coin, and it travelled across the region on the coin's back.

It is blunt and it is not rude. Asking whether somebody has \te{డబ్బు} today is an ordinary question in an \te{అంగడి} where the account is settled by the month.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two. And one of them you had already used once.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ḍabbu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ḍabbu}, then \emph{lēdu}, as the phrase you already knew
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{డబ్బు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}money\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dhara]{\te{ధర} (dhara) — a price}

\label{lesson:TE-C72-price}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ḍabbu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ధర}}
\textbf{\te{ధర}} (\emph{dhara}) — \textquotedblleft{}a price\textquotedblright{}.

\te{ధర} is a price — what a thing costs, said out loud.

It is Sanskrit, from a sense of what holds a thing up, which is a fair picture of value. Telugu uses it for one thing's price and for prices in general: when people say the \te{ధర} has gone up, they mean everything has.

Asking is direct and expected. Nobody in an \te{అంగడి} minds the question, and asking before you pick a thing up is politer than asking after.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three. The question you are allowed to ask first.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dhara}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dhara}, then \emph{ḍabbu}, in the order they come up
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ధర} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a price\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tūkaṁ]{\te{తూకం} (tūkaṁ) — weight}

\label{lesson:TE-C72-weight}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{dhara} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తూకం}}
\textbf{\te{తూకం}} (\emph{tūkaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}weight\textquotedblright{}.

\te{తూకం} is weight — what the scales say, and also the act of weighing.

Almost everything in an \te{అంగడి} is sold by it: \te{బియ్యం}, \te{ఉప్పు}, \te{చక్కెర}, \te{మిరప}. The \te{ధర} you are quoted is a \te{ధర} for a \te{తూకం}, so the two words travel together.

It carries fairness as well. Somebody who speaks with \te{తూకం} is somebody whose words are measured, and short \te{తూకం} is a serious accusation.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. What the \te{ధర} is attached to.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tūkaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tūkaṁ}, then \emph{dhara}, as one question in a shop
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{తూకం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}weight\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bēraṁ]{\te{బేరం} (bēraṁ) — a bargain, haggling}

\label{lesson:TE-C72-bargain}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tūkaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{బేరం}}
\textbf{\te{బేరం}} (\emph{bēraṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bargain, haggling\textquotedblright{}.

\te{బేరం} is the haggle — the back and forth between the \te{ధర} asked and the \te{ధర} paid, and also the deal that comes out of it.

It is expected in an open market crowd and out of place in a fixed-price \te{అంగడి}, and telling those two apart is most of what a newcomer gets wrong.

However the \te{బేరం} ends, it ends with \te{ధన్యవాదములు}, and in a small \te{అంగడి} it ends with both sides fairly sure they did well out of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{అంగడి}, \te{డబ్బు}, \te{ధర}, \te{తూకం}, \te{బేరం}. Enough to buy something and thank the person who sold it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bēraṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then close with \emph{dhanyavādamulu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{బేరం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a bargain, haggling\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
